similar_scenes.name: Country-rock y roots-rock
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: En los setenta, el reajuste a los viejos valores (blues, folk, country) convierte al rock en uno de los mayores éxitos del consumismo: el Establishment ya no intenta destruirlo, lo absorbe. El country-rock de Gram Parsons es una moda enorme: Commander Cody, New Riders Of The Purple Sage, Manassas, Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Poco y los Eagles (Desperado, Hotel California); en Nashville surgen los «outlaws» (Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Kris Kristofferson). El roots-rock sigue con Hot Tuna, Little Feat y Doobie Brothers, y la nostalgia recupera el blues (Roy Buchanan, Bonnie Raitt), la armonía vocal (Manhattan Transfer, Roches, McGarrigle Sisters) y los cincuenta (American Graffiti).

podcast.title: Post-1978 Rock Diversification
podcast.body: Country rock emerged as a distinct genre within mainstream rock discussions after 1978, highlighting the increasing specialization of musical styles. "People were now talking about metal and Prague and folk rock, and soft rock, and country rock, and blues rock, and of course, punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: 1970s and 1980s Impact on Country
podcast.body: Many country music musicians in the 1970s and 1980s believed that rock nearly destroyed country, but the inverse is also suggested: that rock, particularly country rock, "pushed country forward." "many country music musicians in the 70s and in the 80s said that rock nearly killed country it actually seems to me like it may have been the other way around that rock saved country or at the very least it pushed country forward."

srcs.episode: Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock

podcast.title: Artist Dislike for Label
podcast.body: Many 1970s singers and bands labeled as country rock actively disliked the term, preferring alternative descriptors for their blended sound. This aversion reflects the often-unwanted imposition of genre classifications on evolving music. "It is also true that many of the 70s singers and bands that were being labeled as country rock did not like the label."

srcs.episode: Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock
Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock

podcast.title: Blend of Traditional Country and Contemporary Rock
podcast.body: The music attracting attention in Austin during the 1970s was a mixture of traditional country western and contemporary rock and roll. Willie Nelson and others believed this blend was inevitable due to Austin's unique, liberal-minded audience, especially the university population. "The music that's attracting all this attention is a mixture of traditional country western and contemporary rock and roll, a blend that Willie Nelson and others say had to happen eventually because of Austin's unique audience."

srcs.episode: Ep. 49 - Austin City Limits and the 70s Country Music Revolution

podcast.title: Bridging Audience Appreciation
podcast.body: The fusion of country and rock sounds, driven by both country-oriented rock musicians and innovative country musicians, played a crucial role in cultivating a younger audience's appreciation for country music. This cross-pollination helped bridge a generational and cultural gap. "the authors pointed out that the fusion of country and rock sounds in the way it helped a younger audience develop an appreciation for country music resulted in quote, as much as from the experimentation of country oriented rock musicians as from the innovativeness of country musicians."

srcs.episode: Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock
Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock

podcast.title: Commercial Struggles
podcast.body: Country rock faced significant commercial challenges in the 1970s and 1980s, struggling to achieve big record sales and secure radio airplay. It was often characterized as being "too rock for country" and "too country for rock," highlighting its difficulty fitting into established genre formats. "Country rock has very loyal fans, but it has never been a commercial success."

srcs.episode: Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock
Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock

podcast.title: Cultural Reaction to the 1960s
podcast.body: Country rock was viewed as a symptom of a general cultural reaction to the unsettling 1960s, reflecting a desire to escape the "corrupt present" by returning to a "virtuous past," real or imagined, with a nostalgic country twang resonating on pop charts. "This yend to escape the corrupt present by returning to the virtuous past real or imagined has haunted Americans never more so than today. An nostalgic country twang resounds all up and down the pop charts."

srcs.episode: Ep. 59 - Bands and Booze on the Festival Express of 1970

podcast.title: Eagles' Commercial Success
podcast.body: The Eagles became the most successful country rock band, even as they evolved beyond the genre's initial sound. "the eagles were the most successful of the country rock bands even when they were no longer country rock."

srcs.episode: Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock

podcast.title: Eagles' Evolution Away From Label
podcast.body: Don Henley expressed the Eagles' desire in 1974 to move away from the "country rock label" and the "ballad syndrome" to a harder rock sound, particularly after Don Felder joined. "he said we like to be a nice little country rock band from Los Angeles about half the time we wanted to get away from the ballad syndrome."

srcs.episode: Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock

podcast.title: Folk Influences and Evolution
podcast.body: The country rock sound, with Jerry Jeff Walker as one of its originators, was heavily influenced by folk music and subsequently evolved into the Outlaw Country or Progressive Country movements of the 1970s. "Walker is one of the originators of the country rock sound, which is very much influenced by folk and that kind of evolves into this."

srcs.episode: Ep. 46 - The Chaos and Music of the Ozark Music Festival of 1974

podcast.title: Greg Ball's Genre
podcast.body: Greg Ball, an artist from Kingston who had a record produced by Paul Langlois of The Tragically Hip, is identified as a "country rock guy." "Paul Langwaw produced a record for Greg Ball, a country rock guy from Kingston."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Gord Downie: A Remembrance Part 2

podcast.title: Kansas City's Spiritual Home
podcast.body: Rock journalism legend Greg Shaw considered Kansas City to be the "spiritual home of country rock." The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band is a prime example of a band that would now be categorized under this genre. "Greg Shaw wrote that Kansas City was like the spiritual home of country rock."

srcs.episode: Ep. 46 - The Chaos and Music of the Ozark Music Festival of 1974

podcast.title: Linda Ronstadt's Influence on Popularity (1970s)
podcast.body: Linda Ronstadt significantly contributed to making country rock popular in the 1970s. Her unique fusion of country and rock elements was instrumental in making country music cool and accessible to many young rock enthusiasts. "she helped make country cool for a lot of young rock fans with her blend of country rock."

srcs.episode: Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire

podcast.title: Poco's DNA
podcast.body: Poco's influence and musical DNA are recognized as foundational to country rock, similar to Gram Parsons, even if they did not achieve equivalent mainstream fame. "the band goes influence on country rock is similar to that of Graham Parsons the DNA is there."

srcs.episode: Ep. 35 - Cosmic American Music - 70s Country Rock

podcast.title: Poor Production in Early Country Rock
podcast.body: Glenn Frey noted that early country rock records often "did not sound good" and were "poorly produced," which prompted The Eagles to seek out a British producer for an edgier sound. "the records from those bands did not sound good they were poorly produced so they turned to British producer Glenn Johns looking for an edgy or sound."
